sections.title: How does the Angle of refraction calculator work?
sections.html:
The Angle of refraction calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle of incidence (θ₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the medium 1 and the medium 2); then you type in the angle of refraction (θ₂) and the Angle of incidence (θ₁) print.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Angle of refraction calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle of incidence (θ₁)=(refractive index 2 (n₂) × the sine of (angle of refraction (θ₂)) ÷ refractive index 1 (n₁))
Refractive index 2 (n₂)=refractive index 1 (n₁) × the sine of (Angle of incidence (θ₁) print)
A 2 print=(refractive index 1 (n₁) ÷ refractive index 2 (n₂))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Medium 1 set to Vacuum, Refractive index 1 (n₁) = 10, Medium set to Air and Refractive index 2 (n₂) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Angle of incidence (θ₁) = 10 deg, A 1 print = 90 deg and A 2 print = 90 deg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angle of incidence (θ₁) = 10 deg, A 1 print = 90 deg and A 2 print = 90 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Medium 1 set to Vacuum and Refractive index 1 (n₁) = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Angle of refraction calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the angle of refraction and the Angle of incidence (θ₁) print — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Angle of refraction calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle of incidence (θ₁), derived from the angle of refraction and the A 1 print. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Angle of refraction calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the angle of refraction and the A 1 print, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle of incidence (θ₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle of incidence (θ₁) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angle of incidence (θ₁) = 10 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Angle of refraction calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
